lesson.title: Land for Cotton: Congress Orders Native Nations West
lesson.summary: Signed by Jackson in 1830, the Indian Removal Act authorized treaties exchanging Southeastern Native land for territory west of the Mississippi, opening the door to forced removals over the following decade.
lesson.body:
On May 28, 1830, President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act, a law that authorized the federal government to negotiate treaties exchanging Native American land in the Southeast for territory west of the Mississippi River. Although framed as voluntary, the law set in motion one of the most sweeping and coercive displacements of a population in American history.

The law targeted the nations often called the Five Civilized Tribes by white Americans of the time, the Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole, who lived across present day Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, and Florida and had adopted many aspects of European American life, including written constitutions and, in the Cherokee case, a written language developed by Sequoyah. White settlers and state governments coveted their land for cotton cultivation, especially after the cotton gin made growing short staple cotton highly profitable across the Deep South. Pressure intensified further after gold was discovered on Cherokee land in northern Georgia in 1828, setting off a rush of prospectors and squatters.

Georgia in particular passed laws asserting state authority over Cherokee territory and its residents, and the Cherokee Nation sued to block these laws, taking their case to the Supreme Court. In Worcester v. Georgia in 1832, Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that the Cherokee Nation was a sovereign entity and that Georgia's laws had no force within its territory. Jackson, who supported Georgia's position and removal policy generally, did not enforce the ruling, and while a famous line attributed to him, that Marshall had made his decision and could now enforce it himself, may be apocryphal, his administration's inaction had the same practical effect of leaving the Cherokee unprotected.

Removal proceeded through a series of treaties, some negotiated in bad faith and imposed on unwilling or unrepresentative factions of tribal leadership. The Choctaw were removed first, beginning in 1831, under the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, enduring brutal winter marches with inadequate food and supplies that one Choctaw leader reportedly described in terms close to a trail of tears and death, a phrase that later became attached most famously to the Cherokee removal. Jackson, consistent with the aggressive stance toward Native nations he had shown since his military campaigns against the Creek and Seminole, pushed the policy forward with little regard for the suffering it caused.

The Indian Removal Act reshaped the map of the American Southeast, opening enormous tracts of land to white settlement and cotton plantations while permanently displacing tens of thousands of Native people to what became known as Indian Territory, in present day Oklahoma. Its most devastating single episode came a few years later, after Jackson had left office, when the Cherokee Nation itself was forcibly marched west in the removal remembered as the Trail of Tears.
